title: This Beetle Turns From Green to Black in the Rain. No Paint Involved
subject: hercules beetle

scenes.text: This beetle changes color, and it doesn't use a single drop of pigment.
The male Hercules beetle can reach seven inches long with its horn. In dry air, its wing covers look olive green.
When the air gets humid, the green fades and the shell goes black.
Under the surface sits a layer full of tiny holes. When dry, they hold air, and that layer bounces green light back at you.
In humid air, water seeps into those holes. The green reflection disappears, and the shell looks black.
So the color isn't paint. It's air or water, trapped in holes thinner than a hair.

description:
The Hercules beetle turns from olive green to black, and no pigment is involved.
A layer of tiny holes under its shell holds air when dry and water when humid, which changes the light it reflects.
Would you have guessed the color was just air and water?
first_comment: The color comes from a porous layer about 3 micrometers under the shell. Dry holes reflect green, wet holes go dark. What other animal color trick should we cover next?
